activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: You can keep the beat by tapping your knees, stamping your feet or tapping a drum.
story:
Jaxon went to Milo's house. Milo had a big drum on the floor. It was red like a rainbow stripe. "Want to sing?" Milo asked. "Yes!" said Jaxon.

They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Milo clapped his hands to the beat. Jaxon clapped too. One, two, one, two. But his hands got tired. They hurt a little. Jaxon stopped and looked at his hands. Now what?

Then he had an idea. He stamped his feet instead. One, two, one, two. His feet made the beat! "Look, Milo!" he said. "My feet can do it!" Milo tapped the drum, and it made the beat too. Boom, boom, boom. Jaxon tapped his knees. Tap, tap, tap. That made the beat as well.

They sang the whole song from the start to the end. Jaxon did not forget one word. He stamped, tapped his knees, and Milo hit the drum. Boom, tap, stomp. "Again!" said Jaxon.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Teams warm up by running or stretching before a game.
story:
Benjamin ran out to the backyard. Today was his first soccer game. He was on the blue team. He wanted to kick the ball right away.

The coach called everyone to the grass. "Time to warm up," she said. Benjamin did not want to wait. He reached for the ball. His legs felt stiff like a sleepy caterpillar.

So Benjamin joined the line. The team ran in a big circle. They touched their toes and stretched up high. A butterfly flew by, and Benjamin laughed.

Then the game began. Benjamin ran fast. He kicked the ball far. His legs felt loose and strong. After the game, the coach gave him a juicy orange slice. "Good running today," she said. Benjamin smiled and took a big bite.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Cutting a square from one corner to the opposite corner makes two triangles.
story:
Wyatt sat at the art table. He wanted to make a paper sailboat. His boat needed a triangle sail. But Wyatt only had a square.

"Oh no," said Wyatt. He felt upset. "I need two triangles."

Miss Ana came over. "I can help," she said. She took the square. She took the scissors. She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open. Two triangles! Wyatt clapped his hands.

"My turn to try," said Wyatt. Miss Ana gave him a new square. She held the scissors with him. Snip, snip. Two more triangles!

Wyatt picked a big triangle for the sail. He glued it on the boat. Then he glued a circle for the sun. He glued a square window and a rectangle door.

A cat walked past the window. Wyatt planted his boat on the shelf.

"Look, Miss Ana!" said Wyatt. "My boat has a triangle sail!"

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Dress-up clothes help you pretend to be someone else.
story:
Hazel wants to play firefighter with Ben. But she does not feel like a firefighter yet. Ben has the big red hat. He gets to squirt the hose. Hazel just holds the bucket.

"Can I have a hat too?" she asks. Miss Jo looks in the dress-up box. She finds a little red hat. She sets it on Hazel's head.

Hazel looks in the mirror. "Now I am a firefighter!" she yells, loud at first, then soft. Ben walks slow like a firefighter. Hazel walks slow too. They march around the middle of the rug.

Then Baby Bear needs help. Baby Bear is stuck on the toy chair. "A firefighter can save him!" says Hazel. She climbs the two small steps. She holds Baby Bear close. She pats his head. "You are safe now," she says.

At home time, Hazel gives back the little red hat. "More firefighters tomorrow," says Ben. Hazel smiles and waves. "Me and my hat," she says. "See you tomorrow, Baby Bear."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Hosts show a guest where things are, like the towels and the bathroom.
story:
Grandpa came on the big bus. He was staying for a whole week. Ali jumped up and down. "You can sleep in my room!" said Ali. "I will show you everything."

Grandpa had a bath. Then he called out, "Oh no! I cannot find a towel!" Ali ran to the door. "I know where the towels are!" he said. Ali opened the cupboard. "Here, Grandpa! The towels live in here." Grandpa took a big blue one. "You are a good host," said Grandpa. "A host shows a guest where things are." Ali stood very tall.

So Ali showed Grandpa more things. "Here is the bathroom. Here is your cup. Here is my tidy toy box." Grandpa smiled and smiled. The next morning, Grandpa could not find his socks. Ali looked in the cupboard. He found a sock. Then he found something else. "Grandpa! Your hat is in with the towels!" Grandpa laughed. "The bus was bumpy. My hat jumped out!" Grandpa put the hat on Ali's head. It fell down over his eyes. "I can't see!" said Ali. Grandpa laughed. "Then let me hold your hand."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A coach teaches the team and helps the players learn the game.
story:
Clara rides in the car to the ball field. The grass smells green and fresh. Her team wears red shirts. Clara loves her red shirt.

The coach blows a whistle. It sounds loud and high. "Time to play ball," the coach says. Clara runs to the dirt. She does not know where to stand. She stops and looks around.

The coach pats a spot near first base. "Stand right here, Clara," the coach says. "Watch the bat. When the ball comes, you will get it." Clara stands on the spot. Her shoes feel dusty and warm. She waits. It is quiet for a moment. Then a bat goes crack. The ball rolls toward her. Clara bends down and picks it up. She holds it high.

"Good job, Clara!" the coach calls. Clara smiles big. The coach shows Sam where to stand next. Clara claps for Sam. The team plays until the sun goes soft and orange.

"Same time next week," the coach says. Clara waves her glove in the air.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help your body calm down when you feel angry.
story:
Luka went to the library with his dad. He was excited to find a book about trucks. He ran to the shelf. But the truck book was gone. A girl had it in her hands. Luka felt angry. He stomped his foot and made a loud sound. The girl looked scared and held the book tight.

Dad knelt down next to Luka. "Try slow, deep breaths with me," he said. Luka took one big breath in. Then he let it out slowly. He did it again and again. His body began to calm down. His fists were not tight anymore. The girl watched him breathe.

She brought the book over. "We can share it," she said. Luka smiled. He was happy now. They sat together at a low table. Luka read about a big red fire truck. The girl pointed at a dog in the picture. They laughed at the sweet little dog drinking water. "Friends can wake up a sleepy story time," the librarian said with a smile. Luka turned the page.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: The last number you say when counting tells how many there are altogether.
story:
It was a summer morning at the community centre. Sienna ran to the craft table. "Crackers!" she said. There were two bowls of crackers.

Teacher Maya knelt down. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Sienna looked and looked. She could not tell. "I don't know," she said. Her lip began to cry-ready wobble.

"Count them," said Maya.

Sienna pointed at the small bowl. "One, two, three, four." She looked up. "Four!"

Then she counted the big bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six." She bounced. "Six!"

"Six crackers," she said. "Six is more than four!" She held up the big bowl like a trophy.

Outside the window the sky turned stormy, but Sienna did not care. She held out the big bowl to her friend Leo.

"Six crackers," she said. "You take one, and we can count again."

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: A lifeguard's job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it.
story:
Parker stood by the little pool in his backyard. The water was warm. It was green like the grass. "I want to swim," he said. Daddy held his hand.

Parker saw a big chair by the pool. His cousin Lily sat in it. "Why do you sit up there?" Parker asked. "The lifeguard sits up high," Lily said. "I watch the swimmers. I help anyone who needs it."

Parker kicked his feet in the water. Splash! The water made waves. The waves went out and out. "I see the waves," Lily called from her high chair. "You are swimming!" Parker chased a green ball across the pool. It slipped away. Lily saw him stretch and reach. "I need help," Parker said. Lily climbed down fast and held the ball for him. "Thank you," said Parker. Then it was time for lunch under the big tree.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Long and short are opposites.
story:
Emily wanted to wear her scarf today. It was cold outside. Her scarf was red and soft. Daddy got his scarf too. His scarf was blue and long.

"Look," said Emily. She held up her scarf. It was small. It went up to her knees. Daddy put his scarf on. It went down past his coat.

"Mine is short," said Emily. "Yours is long."

"Yes," said Daddy. "Long and short are opposites."

Emily spun around fast, then stopped slow. The long scarf flapped like a tail. Could a scarf swim in the wind? She waved it and it swished. The pot on the stove made steam. Mommy stirred it. "Hot," said Mommy. "Stay back."

Emily touched the cold window. "Brrr!" Then she found Daddy's old mitten on the shelf. It was tiny. It had been his when he was small!

"Is that true?" Emily asked. Daddy laughed. "Really true," he said.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout.
story:
Milo went to the farmers' market with Dad. He saw big red tomatoes and long orange carrots. "I want to grow my own," said Milo. Dad bought three little seeds and a small pot.

At home, Dad helped Milo put soil in the pot. Milo pushed the seeds down into the dark dirt. He gave them a drink of water. Then he had to wait. Every day Milo stood by the pot. Every day the pot looked the same. "Where are my plants?" he asked. "Soon," said Dad. "Keep the pot near the window, and keep waiting."

Many days went by. Then one morning, Milo looked at the pot. Something small and green was poking up out of the soil. Milo ran to Dad. "A little green thing came up!" he said. Dad smiled. "That is called a sprout," said Dad. "A sprout!" said Milo. He touched the pot softly, very gently, like petting a bird in its nest. Then he got more water for his sprout.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: If you lose something in a busy place, you tell your grown-up instead of going to search by yourself.
story:
Hunter ran to the school playground. He put his hand in his pocket. His little blue dinosaur was not there.

"Oh no," said Hunter. "Where is my dinosaur?" He wanted to run far away and look all alone. Then he saw his teacher, Miss Amy. She was standing by the gate.

"Miss Amy, my dinosaur is lost," said Hunter. "Can you help me look?" Miss Amy smiled a kind smile. "Yes, Hunter. We will search together. That is the safe thing to do." So they did not look apart. They looked side by side.

They peeked under the slide. No dinosaur. They peeked in the sandbox. No dinosaur. Then Miss Amy looked by the swings. "Hunter, come here!" There was the blue dinosaur, sitting on the big red ball. Hunter hugged him close. "You found him because we looked together," said Hunter. "May I pretend he is flying now?" Miss Amy laughed. "Yes, you may." Hunter held his dinosaur up to the sky.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
story:
Daniel sat in his car seat. He held his doll tight. "Are we there now?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. "We will get there later." Mama pulled the car past one tree. Then two trees. Then three trees.

"Is it later yet?" asked Daniel. "Is it later now?"

"Later means some time after now," said Mama. "Not right away."

Daniel looked out the window. Now he saw a red truck. Now he saw a cow. Now the cow was gone, like it was lost behind the hill.

"Is it later yet?" he asked again. They passed four trees. Then five.

"Yes," said Mama. "Now it is later. We are here today, just like we said."

Daniel hugged his doll. He clapped his hands. "Later came after now!"

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: After playing outside or petting an animal, it is time to wash your hands.
story:
Felix was in the kitchen. His tummy was rumbling. Lunch was coming soon.

First, Felix ran outside to the yard. He patted the big brown dog. The dog licked his hand. "Stinky dog," Felix said with a giggle.

Then Felix came back in. He sat down at the table. Mama put bread and cheese on a plate. Felix reached for the bread.

"Wait," said Mama. "Where did your hands just be?"

Felix looked at his hands. He thought for a moment. "On the dog," he said. "I patted the dog!"

"What do we do after we pet an animal?" asked Mama.

Felix wondered. Then he jumped down. "Wash hands!" he said. "Wash, wash, wash!"

He ran to the sink. Mama turned on the water. Felix pushed the soap pump. Bubbles grew on his hands. "Bubbles!" he said.

Mama helped him rub. They rubbed and rubbed. "Sing the song," said Mama. Felix sang his counting song. When the song was done, the hands were done.

Mama held a towel. Felix dried his hands, one at a time. His hands smelled like soap now. Not like dog at all.

Felix climbed back to his seat. He picked up the bread. "Yum," he said, and took a big bite.

After lunch, Mama said, "Potty time." Felix ran to the bathroom. He stopped and looked back.

"Wash, wash, wash," he said to himself. And he did.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: If your shirt gets caught in the zipper, pulling the zipper back down a little can free it.
story:
Chloe was in the kitchen. Her coat was on the chair. She wanted to put it on all by herself. Her mom was making soup, so Chloe had time to try.

She pushed her arms in. The coat felt big and warm. Then she pulled the zipper up. It went up, up, then it stopped. The zipper was stuck! It had caught her sweater. "Oh no," said Chloe.

Her mom came close and watched. Chloe did not pull hard. She pulled the zipper back down, just a little. The sweater came free. The zipper slid up again, all the way to her chin. Chloe smiled. "I did it!" she said. She hid her hands in her sleeves, then popped them out. "I'm a wild kitty," she said, and she patted the wooden table with her mittens.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A number word always means the same amount: 'three' always means three things.
story:
Alexis lived in the city, but today he was at Grandpa's house. It was a rainy day. His socks were warm and dry inside.

"Can I have some grapes?" Alexis asked.

"You can have three," said Grandpa.

Alexis looked at the bowl. He picked one big grape. He picked two small ones. He looked at his hand.

"Grandpa, do big grapes count as more?"

"No," said Grandpa. "One grape is one. Three grapes are three."

Alexis put one big grape on the plate. Then he put one more. Then one more. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three."

"Three!" said Grandpa.

Then Grandpa said, "Let's clap for the cookies. They need ten minutes in the oven." Grandpa set the timer. Alexis clapped while they waited.

The timer rang. Grandpa took out the cookies. Alexis counted them on the plate.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

He gave one warm cookie to Grandpa first.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: The last place you remember having something is a good place to start looking.
story:
Abigail lost her bunny. The bunny was her favorite toy. She looked under her bed. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. No bunny there either.

Abigail looked behind the big chair. She found a dust ball and one sock. Still no bunny. Her tummy felt sad. She sat down on the rug.

Then she thought hard. "When did I hold bunny last?" she said. "I had bunny at snack time. I ate my apple." She ran to the snack table. There was her chair. There was her cup. And there, under the chair, was bunny! Bunny had slid down when she ate.

Abigail hugged bunny tight. "I found you," she said. "You were near the last snack spot."

Mama came in. "There you are," said Mama. "You look happy." Abigail held up bunny. "Bunny was hiding by my chair," she said. Mama smiled. "Good thinking. Now let's clean up the crumbs."

Abigail helped wipe the table. Then she put bunny on her lap. She gave bunny a kiss on the soft ear. "Next time I will look here first," she whispered. Bunny's ear flopped over, real and warm, as they both slid off the chair to play.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day.
story:
Ellie went to the pet store with her dad. She saw fish, birds, and one small gray kitten. "Can we take her home?" Ellie asked. "Yes," said Dad. "She will be ours to care for."

At home, the kitten drank from her little bowl. Then she went to sleep. Ellie played with her toys on the playground mat. Later, the kitten came back to the bowl. She sniffed it. She turned away.

"Why won't she drink?" Ellie asked. Dad looked in the bowl. "The water is all gone," he said. "Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day." Dad held the bowl. Ellie helped him fill it with clean water from the tap. The kitten ran over. She drank and drank.

The next morning, Ellie looked at the bowl first thing. It was empty again. She carried it to Dad. "She needs new water," said Ellie. Dad filled it up. The kitten purred and rubbed Ellie's leg. "I'm sorry it was empty," Ellie whispered. The kitten drank, then chased her tail.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours.
story:
Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. There were only three pots. "One, two, three," he counted. A red pot. A yellow pot. A blue pot.

Dad sat on the grass with him. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," said Dad. Leon tapped each pot. "Red, yellow, blue," he said. "Red, yellow, blue." But where were the other rainbow colours? Leon felt sorry for his rainbow. A rainbow needs more colours.

He dipped his brush in the red pot. He dipped it in the yellow pot too. He swirled the brush on the paper. The paint turned orange! Leon gasped. Red and yellow made orange. Next he mixed blue and yellow. The paint turned green, green like the grass. He mixed red and blue. The paint turned purple, purple like a plum.

Leon painted a big rainbow. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. He held it up to the sky. "Look, Dad! My rainbow!" The paper did not sink. It waved in the soft wind, bright as the ocean in a story. Dad clapped his hands. "Paint it again," he said. So Leon dipped his brush in the red pot once more.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Families pack clothes that fit the weather where they are going, like a swimsuit for the beach or a warm coat for the snow.
story:
Connor was three years old. He was going on a big trip. His family drove a long, long way. Then they walked into a hotel room. "We are here!" Connor yelled.

Connor opened his little brown bag. He pulled out his swimsuit. "Beach time!" he said. But when he looked out the window, he saw white snow. Lots and lots of snow. Big flakes fell on the glass.

Daddy laughed softly. "We packed warm coats, not swimsuits," he said. "Snowy places need mittens and boots." He helped Connor find his red mittens. Mommy helped too. She zipped up his puffy coat.

Then Connor saw something. He put on his mittens, and his hands got warm. His coat went on, and his whole body got warm. Warm clothes for snow. Swimsuits were for sunny beach days.

Connor ran to the window. He pressed one mitten hand on the cold glass. "Bye bye, snowflake," he whispered. The little white dot melted away under his warm, red mitten.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, players try to get the ball into the net to score a goal.
story:
Aiden sat on Grandpa's big soft couch. The room smelled like popcorn. Uncle Ben handed Aiden a warm bowl, but Grandpa held it first, so it would not be too hot.

On the TV, men ran fast on green grass. Aiden saw a big white net. "The ball must go over the net," Aiden said. He pointed with one small finger at the screen.

A player kicked the ball. It went low. It went under the bar and into the net. The crowd on TV jumped up. Everyone in the room jumped too. "Goal!" they shouted. Aunt Maya clapped so loud. "Goal! The ball went in the net!"

Aiden clapped too. "In the net! Goal!" He counted on his fingers. "One goal. Two goals. Three goals." Each time a ball went in, everyone cheered.

Later Grandpa set out paper and red paint. "Can you paint a goal?" he asked. Aiden painted a green field. He painted a net with a ball inside it. He dipped his finger in the paint and made a dot right in the net. Uncle Ben looked at the painting and laughed. "That one is a goal too," he said.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: A grown-up should check that the water is warm, not hot, before you wash.
story:
Hayden went to the pharmacy with his mom. His tummy felt funny, so they picked up some medicine. The pharmacist said, "Wash your hands well, okay?" Hayden nodded. He wanted to be a good hand washer.

At the bathroom sink, Hayden reached for the tap. Mom stopped him fast. "Wait. Let me check the water first." She put her hand under it. "It is too hot. We need warm, not hot." She turned the tap a little. "Now it is warm." Hayden put his hands in. It felt nice, like soft rain on his fingers.

Mom said, "Now soap. We count to twenty." Hayden rubbed the soap. One, two, three. Bubbles grew on his hands. Four, five, six. He made a bubble shadow on the wall. Seven, eight, nine. Mom held the next towel ready for him. They counted all the way. Ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty. "Rinse!" said Mom. Hayden rinsed the bubbles away. His hands were clean and shiny. "All done," he said, and held them out for the towel.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: Singing a song again and again helps you learn its words by heart.
story:
Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Beth played a song on her small drum. Boom, boom, boom. All the children clapped along. Eva clapped too. Boom, boom, boom.

Then Miss Beth sang a rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Eva opened her mouth. But the second line was gone. It would not come out. "Where did the words go?" Eva asked. Miss Beth smiled. "Let's sing it again and see."

So they sang it again. And again. And again. Each time, Eva sang more words. Soon she knew the whole rhyme. She had sung it so many times that the words stayed in her head, all by themselves.

Miss Beth counted the claps. "Let's clap a big number," she said. "Ten!" They clapped ten times. Eva sang and clapped at the very same time. It was a huge smile on her face.

"Now I know it by heart," Eva said. She sang the rhyme one more time, all alone, and everyone clapped.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. But he looked in the paint box. No orange! "Oh no," said Weston. "My pumpkin needs orange. Orange is my favorite color."

Grandma set out little cups. Red paint sat in one cup. Yellow paint sat in another cup. Blue paint and green paint sat there too. "Try stirring," said Grandma. Weston dipped his brush in red. He dipped it in yellow too. He stirred and stirred. The paints mixed in the cup. "Grandma! Look! It turned orange!" His brush was orange. His pumpkin was orange. It looked so real and round.

Then Weston tried green and blue. That made a dark color, like the night sky. He giggled. "Paint is like a puzzle," said Grandma. Weston touched the wet pumpkin. It felt cool and slippery. Just then, the paint cup tipped over. Red paint ran across the table like a little river. Grandma laughed and grabbed a towel. "Now the table is red!" she said. Weston held up his orange brush. "I can fix it!"

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: An umbrella keeps rain off your head.
story:
Jackson went to the park with Gran. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jackson wore his hat. A leaf fell from the big tree. The wind blew it round and round. "It is windy," said Gran. Jackson chased the leaf. He laughed when it jumped away.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Jackson felt drops on his nose. "Oh no, my hat is wet," he said. Gran opened her big umbrella. She held it over Jackson's head. The rain could not get him anymore. His hair stayed dry. "Come close," said Gran. They shared the umbrella. It kept the rain off both of them.

They walked home under it together. Jackson pointed at a picture on a wall. It showed kids in snow boots and mittens. "When it is snowy, you wear warm clothes," said Gran. Jackson hoped it would snow soon. He would wear his red mittens. For now, he stayed cozy under the umbrella. "Hold my hand," said Gran. Jackson squeezed it tight.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Pressing too hard on a pencil can break its tip.
story:
Wren sat at the big table. She had a paper and a pencil. She wanted to write her name all alone.

Mama sat next to her. "Hold the pencil like this," said Mama. She showed Wren how to pinch it near the tip. Wren tried. Her fingers felt funny at first.

Wren pressed down hard. She made a big W. Then she made an R. But the R was dark and thick. SNAP! The pencil tip broke off. The point was gone.

"Uh oh," said Wren. "Why did it break?"

"You pressed too hard," said Mama. "Try pressing soft and gentle."

Mama turned the pencil in the sharpener. The tip came back, new and pointy. Wren held it again. This time she pressed light, like a feather on the paper. She wrote W, then R, then E, then N. No snap. The letters sat on the line in a row.

Wren smiled at Mama's face. "Look! I did it all alone!"

"Yes you did," said Mama. She gave Wren a hug. Wren wrote her name one more time, soft and slow, all by herself.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A teacher is the grown-up who looks after and helps the children in a class.
story:
Jasmine stood in the big school cafeteria. She held her tray with both hands. On the tray was a tasty apple and a cup of milk.

Jasmine saw a boy with a red shirt. He looked shy, just like her. He whispered, "Who is that lady?"

"That is my teacher," Jasmine said. "Teachers help the children in a class."

The boy smiled a little smile. Then he walked to the teacher and said, "Hello." The teacher said, "Hello! I am Miss Kim." She took his tray and set it on the table so his hands were free.

Jasmine wanted to say hello too. But her milk tipped over. Plop! The milk made a big white puddle on the table.

"Uh oh," said Jasmine. "What will we do?"

Miss Kim came with a cloth from the kitchen. She wiped the table. Wipe, wipe, wipe. The puddle went away and the table was dry. "Now you can skip to your seat," said Miss Kim.

Jasmine skipped all the way to the table. She sat next to the boy with the red shirt. "Hello, I am Jasmine," she said.

"Hello, I am Sam," he said. "Your apple looks tasty."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Friends playing pretend together can agree on what happens next.
story:
Arthur ran up to Ben's door. He could not wait to play.

"I have a big dragon," said Ben. "He is green and scary!"

"No," said Arthur. "My dragon is friendly. He helps people."

Ben frowned. Arthur frowned too. Now what?

"Wait," said Ben. "Can our dragon be both? Scary to bad guys, and friendly to us?"

"Yes!" said Arthur. "Let's say he is friendly, but very big."

They shook hands. The dragon was friendly and very big. Arthur clapped.

Then Arthur saw a blue blanket on a chair. He put it in a basket. He made a soft round nest. The dragon could sleep there!

"Now the dragon is a baby," said Arthur.

"Then we must feed him," said Ben.

Ben got a cup of water from the sink. His mom watched and helped him pour. Arthur held a spoon very carefully.

The baby dragon yawned. He went to sleep in the nest.

Arthur whispered, "Shh. The baby is sleeping."

Ben whispered too, "Can a baby dragon fly?"

"Not yet," Arthur whispered back. "First he has to grow big."

They sat by the nest. They waited for their friendly dragon to grow.

"Here, dragon," said Arthur softly. "Wake up soon."

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in.
story:
Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His plate was full of rice. He took a big bite and chewed slowly.

"Dada," he said, "can I sleep in my party shirt tonight? It has gold stars on it."

Mama smiled. "Party shirts are for parties," she said. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in."

"But I love the gold stars," said Muhammad.

After dinner, Mama filled the tub with warm water. Muhammad had a bath. He splashed a little and washed his toes. Then Dada helped him dry off with the big soft towel.

Muhammad ran to his room. His party shirt hung on the chair by his desk. He touched the gold stars one more time. Then he looked at his drawer. It was open. Inside were his soft blue pajamas with little moons.

He put on the pajamas. They felt warm and cozy. He climbed into bed and pulled the blanket up.

"Mama," he said, "the stars can wait for a party. My moons are here now."

"Good night, Muhammad," Mama said. She turned off the light.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: People say thank you when someone gives them a present.
story:
Maya turned four today. Her party was at the park. There was a big table with cake. Her grandma stood near the cake. There were balloons and a song.

Maya sat by the presents. Her friend Ben gave her a red truck. Maya opened it fast. Then she saw a shiny box. She jumped up and ran to it. Grandma put a hand on her arm. "Did you say something to Ben?" she asked. Maya looked back at Ben. He was looking at the ground. Maya ran back to him. "Thank you for the truck," she said. Ben smiled big. "You can push it with me," he said. They pushed the truck down the hill together. It did not spill anyone's juice. Maya asked, "Is the juice okay?" Ben said, "Yes, it is fine."

Later Maya felt too excited to sit. She spun around and got dizzy. "I feel sick," she said. Grandma held her hand. "Sit with me and breathe," Grandma said. Maya sat. Soon she felt better.

The cake had four candles. Dad lit them with a match. Maya watched from her chair. She made a wish. Then she blew out the candles. Everyone clapped. Ben handed her a piece of cake. Maya looked up at him. "Thank you," she said. Ben giggled and gave her a high five.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Things can end up inside other things, like a toy tucked in a bag or coat pocket.
story:
Hazel went to the grocery store with Dad. She carried her little bunny in the cart. The cart went slow down each aisle. Hazel looked at the apples. Then she looked down at the cart. Bunny was gone.

"Bunny is lost," said Hazel. She looked under the bread. No bunny. She looked behind the milk. No bunny. Dad looked too. The store had so many shelves and so many boxes.

Then Hazel saw a big pile of paper bags. Things can end up inside other things, she thought. She peeked into a bag by the carrots. Something soft was in there. It was bunny! Bunny had been tucked in the bag all along. "I found you," said Hazel. She gave bunny a big hug.

Dad put the apples in a bag too. The bag made a crunchy sound. Hazel laughed and held bunny tight. "One more aisle," said Dad. "Let's go slow," said Hazel. Bunny rode home on her lap.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out.
story:
Athena ran out to the backyard. Dad sat on the step with his tea. "Stay where I can see you," he said. Athena chased a yellow leaf past the swing. Then she saw something neat at the far fence. A train went by there! She wanted to count the cars.

She ran toward the fence. The grass was cold and wet on her toes. She looked back. She could not see Dad. The big hedge was in the way. Athena stopped. Her tummy felt small and tight.

Then she heard Dad's voice. "Athena? I cannot see you!" She ran back fast. The grass whooshed under her feet. There was Dad, waving from the step. She could see him again. He could see her too.

"You went too far," said Dad. "Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out." Athena held his hand. It felt warm. Her toes felt cold. "Warm hand, cold toes," she said. Dad laughed.

They sat together on the step. The train went by again. Choo, choo! Athena counted the cars. "One, two, three, four!" Dad kissed the top of her head. The tea was hot, so Dad held it. Athena snuggled close. "Stay where you can see me," she said. "Yes," said Dad. "Right here."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: After a shot, the nurse may put a small bandage over the spot.
story:
Ellie sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. "Will the shot hurt?" she asked. "Just a tiny pinch," said Mommy. "Then we get ice cream."

The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick pinch! It was done. Then the nurse did a new thing. She put a small bandage over the spot on Ellie's arm. "You can pick one," said the nurse. Ellie saw a red bandage, a blue bandage, and a bandage with stars. "Stars!" said Ellie. The stars were yellow and shiny. "Mommy, look, one, two, three stars!"

At the ice cream shop, Ellie held up her arm. "My bandage has stars," she said. The girl at the next table looked. "Wow, you are so smart," said Mommy. Ellie licked her pink ice cream. Outside, the rain began to tap on the window. Ellie ate slow, one lick at a time, and the stars stayed dry on her arm.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: Sun, sock and sand all start with the letter S and the 'sss' sound.
story:
Ayla sat in Grandma's cozy reading nook. The window was cloudy outside. Grandma held up a card with a big S on it.

"This is S," said Grandma. "It says sss, like a snake."

Ayla pressed the card to her ear. "It is quiet," she said. Grandma laughed.

"Can you find things that say sss?" asked Grandma. "Let's play a hunt around the room."

Ayla looked. She looked high. She looked low. The sun peeked out from the clouds and made a warm spot on the rug.

"Sun!" said Ayla. "Sss-un. Sun starts with sss!"

Grandma clapped. Ayla pulled off one shoe. "Sock!" she said. She held it up. "Sss-ock. Sock starts with sss too!"

The sand bucket sat by the door. Ayla touched the sand with one finger. It was soft and bumpy. "Sand," she whispered. "Sss-and."

Grandma nodded. "Sun, sock and sand," she said.

Ayla counted on her fingers. "Three things. All S!"

Then she picked up the card again. She looked all around the room. What else could say sss?

"Grandma, what about the snake in your book?"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: People often wear special clothes to a celebration.
story:
Nathan woke up early. Today was the festival day. He stood by his drawer and looked and looked. "I cannot pick," he told Mama. Mama smiled and waited. Nathan pulled out his red shirt. Then he pulled out his blue shirt. He held them both. He waited some more. Then he found it. His yellow shirt with the sun on it. "This one," said Nathan. "It is my special shirt."

At the festival, the street was full. Drums went boom, boom, boom. Nathan smelled sweet popcorn and warm bread. He held Papa's hand. They walked up a little hill to see the whole street. It had rained in the morning. The road was still wet, and the lights danced on it.

Nathan looked around. Grandma wore her long green dress. Papa wore his big white cap. His cousin Maya wore shiny gold bangles. "Everyone has special clothes on," said Nathan. "Just like me." Maya laughed and spun around. Her skirt went round and round. "You look like the sun," she told Nathan. Nathan puffed out his chest. "I am festival sun," he said. And he danced all the way down the hill.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A school day has a time for eating a snack or lunch.
story:
Lea stood at the gate of the school playground. She held her teacher's hand. "I am hungry," said Lea. Her tummy made a little growl.

The teacher smiled. "We will have snack time soon," she said. "First we play." Lea let go of the gate. She ran to the slide. The slide was high, but Lea slid down fast. She laughed. She played with a soft toy animal in the sandbox. She made a big hill of sand.

Then a bell rang. "Snack time," said the teacher. Lea ran to the table and sat down. She grabbed her little cup and took a big drink. She munched on her crackers. "Snack time comes after play," said Lea. The teacher nodded. Lea ate all her snack and smiled.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Borrowed books have to be brought back to the library by a certain day, called the due date.
story:
The bookmobile came to Luna's street. Luna held her mama's hand. Inside, the librarian gave Luna a small card. "Your first library card," she said. "It is a gift for you." Luna picked a book about a red fire truck. She wanted to keep it forever.

"Can I keep the truck book always?" Luna asked. The librarian shook her head. "You bring it back on the due date," she said. "Borrowed books have to come back by that day." Luna frowned. The truck book was hers now, sort of. "Then it is empty?" she asked. "No, you get a new book each time," the librarian said. "Someone else can read the truck book too."

On the due date, Luna put the book in her bag. She and mama walked to the bookmobile. Luna gave the book back. Then a boy took the truck book off the shelf. He smiled big. "Now he gets to move it to his house," Luna said. The librarian handed Luna a new book about a big yellow bus. "Next one, please," said Luna.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Standing closer to the hoop makes it easier to get the beanbag in.
story:
Jasmine stood far from the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It missed. She threw again. It missed again.

Her furry dog, Biscuit, ran to get the beanbag. He gave it a little lick, then dropped it in her hands.

"One, two, three steps," Jasmine counted. She took three steps closer to the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in! She threw it again from the same spot. It went in again.

Then Dad rolled her the big ball. She held out both hands. The ball bumped her tummy, but she caught it.

"Good job," Dad said. "Even a doctor has to practice new things."

Jasmine laughed. She stepped back far from the hoop. "Watch me, Biscuit," she said. She ran closer, and threw.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A tag on a pet's collar tells people how to reach its family if the pet gets lost.
story:
Emile sat in a little chair at the vet. A puppy slept in a basket next to him. The puppy was brown with one white ear. Emile gave the white ear a soft pat.

"Time for a collar," said the vet. She held up a small tag. It was shiny and round. Emile picked it out all by himself. Then the vet asked for his phone number. Emile said it slowly, and his mom helped. The vet put the number on the tag. "Why does the puppy need our number?" Emile asked. Mom smiled. "If the puppy gets lost, the tag tells people how to reach us," she said. The tag went on the collar with a little click.

At home, the puppy ran in the grass. Emile gave him water in a blue bowl. He gave him a kiss on his soft head. "I love you, puppy," Emile said. The tag went glint, glint in the sun. Emile held the tag in his hand and read the number. Then he let the puppy sniff it. The puppy wagged his tail, and they went inside together.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Washable markers wash off skin with soap and water.
story:
Clara sat at the big art table. She was drawing a blue fish. The marker slipped. Now her hand had a blue mark too.

Clara looked at her hand. "Oh no," she said. Would the blue mark stay there forever?

Miss Jo held up Clara's hand. "These are washable markers," she said. She took Clara to the little sink.

Clara put her hand under the water. Miss Jo added soap. Clara rubbed and rubbed. The blue mark began to fade. Then it was gone!

Clara looked at her clean hand. She had made the mark go away. She drew a small green butterfly on her paper. Then she drew a tiny green dot on her other hand. "Watch this," she said to her friend Sam.

Clara washed her hand again. Soap, water, rub. The green dot vanished. Sam clapped his hands.

"You can draw a cute fish on me next," said Sam. Clara picked up the orange marker.
